result: The rain began without ceremony, a soft percussion on the leaves that escalated into a steady symphony. I watched from the window, my breath fogging the glass, creating a temporary blur between me and the world. There is a particular kind of solitude in this—the sound of water washing the dust from the day, the smell of wet earth rising through the sill. I thought about how we rush through our lives, collecting moments like stones in a pocket, only to find them weightless later. But this—this simple act of witnessing—felt different. It anchored me. The trees drank greedily, their branches bending in gratitude. A bird, unbothered by the downpour, sang a single defiant note. I could hear the city sigh, its noise muted by the rain's steady insistence. In that moment, I was not anywhere else. I was not thinking of tomorrow or mourning yesterday. I was just here, present, tethered to the rhythm of the falling water. The steam from a forgotten cup of tea curled upward, a ghost of warmth in the cool air, and I let it dissolve along with my worries. When the rain finally slowed to a drizzle, the world felt reborn, washed clean of its hurried edges. I stayed a while longer, listening to the silence that followed, letting it settle into my bones. It was a reminder that the world does not need our permission to be beautiful—it simply is. This, I realized, is the quiet gift of paying attention.
